newsitem.title: USA: Bull spreading seen on USDA Cattle-on-Feed report.
newsitem.headline: Bull spreading seen on USDA Cattle-on-Feed report.

text.p: Chicago Mercantile Exchange cattle traders and livestock analysts look for bull spreading in live cattle futures on Monday following the monthly U.S. Department of Agriculture Cattle-on-Feed Report for major feedlots in the seven key states.
"My feeling is, the February and April (live cattle futures) will probably come to a flat price," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
Analysts called February futures in the live cattle pit on Monday 0.200 cent per lb higher to 0.200 lower while April and June calls were mostly 0.500 to 0.750 cent lower.
Levitt noted that April is currently at a one-cent-per-lb premium to February and heavy placements indicated on the report will be bearish to April and June contracts.

"November placements were the largest on record (for the month). Cattle feeders were optimistic with $70 cattle prices most of the month and feed costs declining" and placed a lot of cattle on feed, Levitt said.
USDA reported the number of cattle in feedlots with capacities of 1,000 head or more on December 1 at 103 percent of last year, near analysts' expectations which had averaged 103.2 percent.

However, November placements on feed were pegged at 108 per cent of a year earlier versus the average trade estimate of 105 percent. November marketings came in at 97 percent, above the average estimate of 93.9.
Marketings were down three percent from last year but were still five percent larger than the 1992-1995 average and should support the February, analysts noted.
However, not all analysts were bearish to the April contract as other parts of the report, especially weight data, could limit pressure in that month.
"If you look at the weight breakdown, we are not really going to see the numbers until May," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.

"You are not going to take these cattle weighing less than 500 lbs or the 600- to 700-lbs and get them on feed and finish by April -- it's just not going to happen because you had too many calves placed on feed," Benson said.

Tom Tippens, chief executive officer of Professional Cattle Consultants Inc, and a panelist on a CME panel after the report, also voiced a more optimistic outlook for early 1997. Most price outlooks are for cash cattle to fall to the $60 per cwt area or lower by next spring and now there is less of a chance of this happening based on the weight, he said.

"The fact that we have been able to pull our slaughter weights down at a time when we probably had the best performance in the history of feedyard performance -- that is something that will carry over into the first quarter," Tippens said. He said there is a "good possibility" that beef output in the first quarter could slipe 2.0 to 2.5 percent.
USDA also on Friday estimated slaughter cattle weights the week ended December 21 at 1,168 lbs, down 32 lbs from average weights a year ago of 1,200.
